catalog_quote: The picture within the Cenderawasih Bay family is somewhat cloudier. Klamer asserts that no more than 14 tonal Austronesian languages have been reported; two, Mor and Ma’ya, are Cenderawasih Bay languages. Dalrymple & Mofu (2012) say only that stress is usually penultimate on polysyllabic words in Dusner; they do not clarify the extent or nature of the variation. Biak stress, according to van den Heuvel (2006), results from the interaction of phonemic vowel length and postlexical rhythmic processes affecting larger phrasal units, rendering it quite variable.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: re-extracted PDF p.118 (printed p. sec. 3.3 'Areal Context' reads exactly as quoted: '..Dalrymple & Mofu (2012) say only that stress is usually penultimate on polysyllabic words in Dusner; they do not clarify the extent or nature of the variation.' The excerpt file matches the PDF verbatim. The following page (p.101) adds nothing further on Dusner (moves to Mor, Ambai). Reading: 'usually penultimate on polysyllabic words' with unspecified exceptions = fixed: penultimate syllable (default/regular penult with a hedge); agree. Status: the first-hand source (Dalrymple & Mofu 2012, LINCOM LW/M 487, print only) was not seen by either reader; Gasser's sentence is an explicit report of…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Dusner usually falls on the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words (per Dalrymple & Mofu 2012 as reported by Gasser); the primary source reportedly hedges with 'usually' without characterising the exceptions.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'usually'; Gasser notes the primary source does not clarify the extent or nature of the variation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement about polysyllabic words; no information on phrase-level prosody or citation forms. This is a second-hand report; the first-hand wording in Dalrymple & Mofu 2012 (phonology chapter) was not seen.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to Dusner of Dusner village, Wandamen Bay (dusn1237); Dalrymple & Mofu's data come from the three remaining speakers (Emma Somesa, Enos Yoweni, Anna Imburi), all also fluent in Wamesa/Wandamen. No dialect differentiation.
